description: Incremental operating-room minutes for IUD insertion performed at the time of bariatric surgery
source: Primary: Children's Hospital Colorado / CU Anschutz adolescent-gynecology 'IUD Placement Under Anesthesia' patient-care protocol (general, non-bariatric IUD-under-anesthesia context), stating the insertion itself takes 5-15 minutes. Corroborating (added 2026-09-11): a retrospective review of 25 patients undergoing concomitant laparoscopic bilateral salpingectomy at the time of primary sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass (12 sleeve, 13 bypass) at a single institution over 6 years found salpingectomy added approximately 10 minutes to operative time (conference abstract, Surgery for Obesity and Related Diseases, April 2026; confirmed via two independent search summaries converging on identical specific details -- direct full-text access returned HTTP 403).
notes: Still no published study of IUD insertion added-time specifically during bariatric surgery. But the salpingectomy finding is a genuine bariatric-surgery-CONTEXT data point (a different minor gynecologic add-on procedure, in an actual bariatric OR, at 12 sleeve/13 bypass cases), and it lands almost exactly on this parameter's existing 10-minute mode, meaningfully increasing confidence in that point estimate even though it is not IUD-specific. If anything, salpingectomy (which involves tubal dissection) plausibly takes longer than simple transcervical IUD placement, so 10 minutes is arguably a conservative (not optimistic) estimate for the IUD case. Evidence tier upgraded from C to B given this corroboration.

description: 12-month probability of levonorgestrel-IUD expulsion when placed as a standalone office procedure (not combined with another surgery)
source: Base value: Masten M, Yi H, Beaty L, Hutchens K, Alaniz V, Buyers E, Moore JM. Body Mass Index and Levonorgestrel Device Expulsion in Adolescents and Young Adults. J Pediatr Adolesc Gynecol. 2024;37(4):407-411. doi:10.1016/j.jpag.2024.03.001 (see notes). High bound: Saito-Tom LY, et al. Levonorgestrel Intrauterine Device Use in Overweight and Obese Women. Hawaii J Med Public Health 2015 (same paper already cited for standalone_office_failure_probability) -- directly re-read 2026-09-11 specifically for its expulsion (not just insertion-difficulty) outcome: 11/145 (8%) overall 12-month expulsion, broken out as 11% normal weight, 4% overweight, 11% obese (P=.47, authors describe the study as underpowered to detect a difference).
notes: Base value kept at Masten's 5.6% because it is the only source with a PAIRED standalone-vs-combined comparison in the same cohort (the differential 3.23x odds ratio this model's whole finding rests on requires that pairing; Saito-Tom has no combined-insertion arm at all, so it cannot speak to the differential). High bound uses Saito-Tom's real adult, obesity-specific standalone expulsion rate (11%) instead of an arbitrary +/-X% band, partially closing the generalizability gap that Masten's cohort is adolescents (ages 10-19), not the adult bariatric-surgery population this model targets. A specific 'class III obesity (BMI>=40), odds ratio 3.06' claim attributable to a search-engine summary was checked directly against Saito-Tom's full text 2026-09-11 and does NOT appear in the paper -- it is not used here; see docs/data_sources.md for that dead end. General LNG-IUS 1-year expulsion in the non-obese general population is reported elsewhere as 3.1%-4.5%, meaningfully lower than either obesity-specific estimate here, externally consistent with obesity/BMI increasing expulsion risk.

description: 12-month probability of levonorgestrel-IUD expulsion when placed at the time of bariatric/metabolic surgery
source: Masten M, Yi H, Beaty L, Hutchens K, Alaniz V, Buyers E, Moore JM. 'Body Mass Index and Levonorgestrel Device Expulsion in Adolescents and Young Adults.' J Pediatr Adolesc Gynecol. 2024;37(4):407-411. doi:10.1016/j.jpag.2024.03.001. PMID 38462038, PMCID PMC11706623 (open access). Directly verified via the full text, 2026-09-10 (retrospective chart review, 588 patients aged 10-19, tertiary children's hospital, 2017-2021). Raw figure: 'Of the patients who concurrently underwent MBS, 16.3% experienced expulsion (7/43).' Table 4 also reports an adjusted odds ratio for this same comparison (MBS vs. non-MBS insertion): OR 3.23, 95% CI 1.11-8.75, P=.024 (adjusted for age, race, ethnicity, insurance, AUB with anemia, and DD indication), see iud_expulsion_odds_ratio_combined_vs_standalone.
notes: Low/high bound is now a real, directly-computed exact (Clopper-Pearson) binomial 95% confidence interval on Masten's own raw proportion (7/43), computed via R's stats::binom.test(7, 43) 2026-09-10: 6.81%-30.70%. Deliberately NOT back-derived from the adjusted OR's CI (1.11-8.75): that OR is adjusted for covariates (age, race, ethnicity, insurance, AUB, DD indication) this project's single-cohort base_value is not, so mixing an adjusted-OR-derived range around an unadjusted point estimate would be internally inconsistent. This closes the gap the one-way sensitivity analysis (analysis/04_sensitivity_analysis.R) surfaced on 2026-09-10: this parameter is used by the cost engine and is the single number most directly responsible for the combined arm's cost disadvantage, yet previously had no sourced uncertainty range at all. The wide CI (driven by the small n=43 combined-arm subgroup) reflects real, not artificial, uncertainty -- this is a retrospective single-center chart review, not a large registry.

description: Adjusted odds ratio for 12-month IUD expulsion, combined bariatric-surgery placement vs. non-combined placement, from Masten et al. 2024's logistic regression
source: Masten M, Yi H, Beaty L, Hutchens K, Alaniz V, Buyers E, Moore JM. J Pediatr Adolesc Gynecol. 2024;37(4):407-411. doi:10.1016/j.jpag.2024.03.001. PMCID PMC11706623 (open access, full text directly verified 2026-09-10, correcting the first author's initial recorded when this row was first added). Table 4, adjusted model: OR 3.23, 95% CI 1.11-8.75, P=.024.
notes: NOT used directly in the cost engine -- provided as a cross-check on iud_expulsion_probability_standalone/_combined above: implied odds ratio from those two probabilities is (0.163/0.837)/(0.056/0.944) = 3.29, closely matching this paper-reported 3.23, which is reassuring internal consistency given _standalone was only approximated. Low/high is this adjusted model's own 95% CI, now directly verified (2026-09-10) rather than recorded as NA; NOT used to derive iud_expulsion_probability_combined's own low/high bound, since that parameter's base_value is the unadjusted raw proportion (7/43) and this OR is adjusted for covariates -- see that parameter's notes for why a same-study, same-scale exact binomial CI was computed instead.

description: Probability that a standalone office IUD-insertion attempt fails outright and must be escalated to a sedated/procedure-suite re-attempt
source: Saito-Tom LY, Soon RA, Harris SC, Salcedo J, Kaneshiro BE. Levonorgestrel Intrauterine Device Use in Overweight and Obese Women. Hawaii J Med Public Health 2015. Retrospective cohort, 149 women (55 normal weight, 45 overweight, 49 obese). Obese group: 4% (2/49) failed insertion, 8% (4/49) 'difficult' insertion; no statistically significant difference by BMI group (P=.47).
notes: Chosen over an alternative source (Harrison, 'Failed IUD insertions in community practice,' Contraception 2012 -- 19.6% failure in nulliparous women choosing emergency contraception, inserted by nurse practitioners without adjuvant measures, at family-planning clinics) because Saito-Tom's obese-BMI-specific population is a much closer match to this project's target population than that emergency-contraception/nulliparous cohort, even though its sample is small (n=49, only 2 failures -- low/high bounds are 0%/8%, the observed failed/difficult rates, not a formal CI). On failure, this model assumes escalation to a sedated re-attempt costing the same added_or_cost as the combined arm's OR/anesthesia minutes, with no duplicate device or professional fee (see R/strategy_costs.R) -- a simplifying assumption, not a sourced escalation-cost figure.

description: Baseline uterine perforation risk per IUD insertion, levonorgestrel-releasing systems specifically, applied identically to both arms
source: Heinemann K, Reed S, Moehner S, Minh TD. 'Risk of uterine perforation with levonorgestrel-releasing and copper intrauterine devices in the European Active Surveillance Study on Intrauterine Devices (EURAS-IUD).' Contraception. 2015;91(4):274-279. doi:10.1016/j.contraception.2015.01.007. Directly verified via the PubMed/Europe PMC abstract, 2026-09-10 (this is the same study Dottino et al. 2016's Table 1 cites for this figure, PMID 25601352): a prospective, multinational cohort of 61,448 women (six European countries, 2006-2013, over 68,000 women-years), 61 perforations among LNG-IUS users, 1.4 per 1,000 insertions (95% CI 1.1-1.8).
notes: NOW WIRED IN (2026-09-10) via compute_expected_perforation_cost() in R/strategy_costs.R, applied identically to both arms -- still NO differential by insertion setting/anesthesia, since evidence on whether concurrent-surgery placement changes perforation risk itself (as opposed to management cost once perforation occurs) remains mixed and inconclusive; see iud_perforation_management_cost's notes for a further, deliberately DEFERRED refinement (EURAS-IUD found perforation is recognized at the time of insertion in only a minority of cases, which could in principle let the combined arm avoid a full separate retrieval episode for that subset -- not yet modeled). This decision not to apply a setting-based risk differential is unchanged from before; what changed is that the risk now has a real cost consequence in the model instead of sitting unused.

description: Cost of managing a perforated IUD (laparoscopic retrieval encounter), applied identically to both arms
source: Dottino JA, Hasselblad V, Secord AA, Myers ER, Chino J, Havrilesky LJ. 'Levonorgestrel Intrauterine Device as an Endometrial Cancer Prevention Strategy in Obese Women: A Cost-Effectiveness Analysis.' Obstet Gynecol. 2016;128(4):747-753, Table 2 (PDF read directly, already used elsewhere in this project for the cancer-prevention module). Dottino et al. sourced this from HCUPnet (Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project), ICD-9 code 998.2 'accidental perforation during procedure,' accessed by Dottino in January 2016, in 2015 dollars: mean $20,805.84, median $14,822.49.
notes: Secondary citation (via Dottino's Table 2), not independently re-queried from HCUPnet directly for this project. Uses the MEAN, not the median, as base_value, since this feeds an expected-value (probability x cost) calculation, where the mean is the correct statistic for a right-skewed cost distribution; low_value is the median as a more conservative reference point; no upper-bound CI was reported by the source, so high_value is left blank rather than fabricated. This almost certainly reflects an ANY-SETTING retrieval episode (typically an interval/office-placed IUD found missing or malpositioned later, escalated to laparoscopic retrieval), not a concurrent-bariatric-surgery-specific scenario. Whether the combined arm could avoid a full separate episode for the minority of perforations recognized at the time of insertion (Heinemann et al. 2015 EURAS-IUD: a minority of cases) is a real, deliberately DEFERRED refinement, not yet modeled -- both arms currently apply this same full cost.

description: NYU Langone Tisch Hospital's published self-pay/discounted-cash price for HCPCS J7297 (levonorgestrel IUD, 52 mg; NYU's file lists Mirena/J7298 and Kyleena/J7296 at the identical $15,304.34 gross / $2,907.82 cash rate, and Skyla/J7301 slightly lower at $12,743.39 gross / $2,421.24 cash), from its CMS-mandated price-transparency machine-readable file
source: NYU Langone Health standard-charges MRF, downloaded directly 2026-09-10, discovered via its cms-hpt.txt auto-discovery file (https://nyulangone.org/cms-hpt.txt -> mrf-url: https://standard-charges-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/pricing_files/133971298-1801992631_nyu-langone-tisch_standardcharges.csv, file dated 2026-01-01). Gross charge $15,304.338, discounted-cash $2,907.82422; across 209 populated commercial-payer negotiated-dollar columns in the same row, min $153.04, median $4,591.30, max $15,304.34 (the maximum equals the gross charge, i.e. at least one payer's contract is charge-based).
notes: Cross-validation only, not used in the base case. NYU's cash price is 3.5x Denver Health's cash price for the same HCPCS code (iud_device_chargemaster_cash_price, $837.67), and its negotiated-rate spread ($153 to $15,304 across 209 payers at one hospital) is itself wider than the entire GPO/340B acquisition-cost range this model uses. This strengthens, rather than undermines, the case for anchoring the base case on GPO/340B acquisition cost instead of any single hospital's charge or cash price: charge and cash prices carry hospital margin and vary enormously by market, while the true acquisition cost is what actually determines the incremental cost difference between strategies.

description: NYU Langone Tisch Hospital's published self-pay/discounted-cash price for CPT 58300 (IUD insertion procedure), from its CMS-mandated price-transparency machine-readable file
source: NYU Langone Health standard-charges MRF, downloaded directly 2026-09-10 (same file and discovery method as iud_j7297_cash_price_nyu_langone). Gross charge $2,152.15, discounted-cash $408.9085, setting listed as 'both' (applies to inpatient and outpatient alike). Across 291 populated commercial-payer negotiated-dollar columns, min $210.08, median $4,100.00, max $25,798.00.
notes: NOT used to update iud_insertion_professional_fee's base value or its $75-$125 low/high bound, which remains an unverified aggregator estimate. NYU's row lists this code's setting as 'both' rather than a professional-only fee, so its price plausibly bundles a facility/OR component that Denver Health (this model's professional-fee source) bills separately; the two figures are not a clean apples-to-apples comparison. Included because it directly informed iud_insertion_professional_fee's Medicaid-scenario override (see R/scenarios.R): the same workbook, parsed worksheet-by-worksheet rather than read as a single printable sheet, also contains the real Colorado CPT 58300 rate ($58.65), resolving a previously-documented gap. description: National Medicaid State Drug Utilization Data (SDUD) 2025 average per-unit reimbursement for Liletta 52 mg (HCPCS J7297/NDC-crosswalked), computed as total dollars reimbursed divided by total units reimbursed across all reporting states, FFS and MCO combined, for calendar-year 2025
source: CMS State Drug Utilization Data 2025, downloaded directly 2026-09-10 from https://download.medicaid.gov/data/sdud2025_updatedjuly2026.csv (discovered via the data.medicaid.gov metastore API, https://data.medicaid.gov/api/1/metastore/schemas/dataset/items). Aggregated 45,877 Liletta prescriptions / 45,988 units reimbursed / $39,437,115.84 total reimbursed across all non-suppressed state-quarter rows (116 of 356 rows were privacy-suppressed for low cell counts and excluded, per CMS convention, not treated as zero). The same file also gives Mirena (243,398 units, $295,346,153.64, avg $1,213.43/unit), Kyleena (22,829 units, $28,479,655.82, avg $1,247.53/unit), and Skyla (4,145 units, $4,407,921.25, avg $1,063.36/unit).
notes: Reference only, not used in the cost model (this is a national reimbursement average, not this model's hospital-specific acquisition-cost or single-state Medicaid framing). Its real value is as the strongest available cross-check on the device-cost figures already in this file: at $857.54, the national Medicaid average for Liletta sits almost exactly between Denver Health's cash price ($837.67), UCLA's negotiated range ($845-$950), and Colorado's own Medicaid PAD rate ($931.73-$978.32), and far below NYU Langone's cash price ($2,907.82). Four independently-sourced, real payer/hospital figures clustering in the same $840-$980 band, with NYU as the clear outlier, is much stronger evidence than any single source that this band, not NYU's, represents typical real-world pricing for this device.

description: Median wage for medical scheduling/administrative staff (SOC 43-6013, Medical Secretaries and Administrative Assistants), per minute
source: O*NET OnLine (https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/43-6013.00), median hourly wage $22.08, attributed to 'Bureau of Labor Statistics 2025 wage data,' directly verified 2026-09-10. Same occupational code and source already used and cited by the sibling emb_colonoscopy project's own coordination_cost/scheduler_hourly_wage_onet_2025 parameters (confirmed by directly reading that project's config/model_parameters.csv, 2026-09-10) -- reused here rather than re-derived, for consistency across both projects. bls.gov itself returns HTTP 403 to automated retrieval (confirmed directly this session); O*NET OnLine is the DOL/BLS-funded site that republishes the same OEWS wage data without blocking it. Converted to per-minute by dividing by 60: 22.08 / 60 = 0.368.
notes: Kept separate from the minutes parameter (combined_arm_scheduling_coordination_minutes) rather than pre-multiplied into a single dollar figure, following this project's existing convention for OR-time costs (combined_arm_added_minutes x direct_room_cost_per_minute, computed in R/strategy_costs.R rather than pre-computed in this CSV) -- the sibling project's own analogous parameter notes flag this decomposition as a preferred future refactor, so building it this way here from the start is the more rigorous choice.

description: Total scheduler labor time to coordinate OR time between the bariatric surgeon and the gynecologist who places the IUD
source: User-provided operational estimate (project owner, 2026-09-10, describing this institution's actual scheduling workflow): each surgeon's own scheduler spends approximately 30 minutes coordinating the combined case (2 schedulers x 30 minutes each = 60 minutes total). This is the same time estimate (2 schedulers x 30 min each) the same project owner previously gave for the sibling emb_colonoscopy project's analogous combined-visit coordination_cost parameter (confirmed by directly reading that project's config/model_parameters.csv, 2026-09-10: 'Time: practitioner estimate (Tyler Muffly, MD, Denver Health)'), so this is a consistent, repeated estimate from the same source, not a one-off guess.
notes: A new cost category for this project: administrative/scheduling coordination overhead specific to needing TWO different physicians' OR time aligned, distinct from the clinical OR-time cost already captured by combined_arm_added_minutes. Applies ONLY to the combined arm -- the standalone arm is a single gynecologist's own routine office visit, requiring no cross-surgeon scheduling coordination. Flagged provisional because the TIME component (30 min/scheduler) is a practitioner estimate, not an independently published or billing-verified figure, even though the WAGE component (surgery_scheduler_wage_per_minute) is real and directly sourced. No low/high range given (unlike the sibling project's own +/-15% wage / +/-50% time modeler-chosen sensitivity bands, which that project's own notes describe as arbitrary widths, not measured uncertainty) -- excluded from analysis/04_sensitivity_analysis.R's sweep for the same reason other unranged-but-used parameters are excluded there.

description: Facility-setting professional fee as a fraction of the office-setting fee for CPT 58300, applied to iud_insertion_professional_fee to get the combined arm's own (first) insertion fee
source: CMS RVU26C (July 2026 National Physician Fee Schedule Relative Value File), CPT 58300 'Insert intrauterine device,' status N (non-covered by Medicare, but RVU components are still published): work RVU 0.98 (same both settings), non-facility (office) practice-expense RVU 2.07, facility (OR) practice-expense RVU 0.22, malpractice RVU 0.11 (same both settings). Non-facility total RVU = 3.16, facility total RVU = 1.31. Ratio = 1.31 / 3.16 = 0.4146. Downloaded directly 2026-09-11 from https://www.cms.gov/files/zip/rvu26c-updated-06-30-2026.zip (file PPRRVU2026_Jul_nonQPP.csv). Stored as a RATIO, applied at compute time to iud_insertion_professional_fee, rather than as its own fixed dollar parameter, so that a scenario overriding iud_insertion_professional_fee (e.g. medicaid_illustrative's Colorado Medicaid rate) automatically produces a consistent facility-equivalent value without needing a second, separately-maintained override -- a ratio is the right representation for a structural, payer-agnostic RVU relationship. Matches the methodology (though not the parameter structure) already established in the sibling emb_colonoscopy project's emb_office_professional_cost/_facility split, confirmed by reading that project's config/model_parameters.csv and docs/data_sources.md directly, 2026-09-11.
notes: Because CPT 58300 is Medicare-non-covered (status N), no live claims-volume data exists to split by place of service the way the sibling project did for the Medicare-covered CPT 58100 (a live CMS PUF query by Place_Of_Srvc); this is a RATIO-based proxy applied to a real anchor price, not itself a directly observed facility-setting charge. Also assumes the office-rate parameter it is applied to is a clean office/nonfacility-equivalent rate, which has not been independently confirmed for either the base case (Denver Health's cash price) or the Medicaid scenario (Colorado's CPT 58300 rate) against either payer's own place-of-service billing logic. Used ONLY for the combined arm's own (first) insertion; iud_insertion_professional_fee (unmultiplied) remains correct for the standalone arm's insertion AND for both arms' replacement-encounter cost, since a replacement is modeled as an office-style encounter regardless of which arm's device expelled (see R/strategy_costs.R).

description: Disposable supply cost for IUD insertion (pelvic exam pack, minimum multi-specialty visit pack, povidone antiseptic solution), applies ONLY to the combined arm
source: CMS CY2026 Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule Direct Practice Expense Inputs file (CMS-1832-F), downloaded directly 2026-09-11 from https://www.cms.gov/files/zip/cy-2026-pfs-final-rule-direct-pe-inputs.zip (file CMS-1832-F_PUF_Supply_508.txt), CPT 58300 nonfacility supply line items, summed: pack, minimum multi-specialty visit (SA048) $4.01 + pack, pelvic exam (SA051) $14.38 + povidone soln/Betadine (SJ041) $0.38/ml x 50ml = $19.00; total $37.39.
notes: Applies ONLY to the combined arm, exactly mirroring the sibling emb_colonoscopy project's emb_disposable_supply_cost treatment for the structurally identical issue (confirmed by reading that project's config/model_parameters.csv and docs/data_sources.md directly, 2026-09-11): all three supply items carry nf_quantity > 0 (priced into iud_insertion_professional_fee, the nonfacility rate the standalone arm uses) but f_quantity = 0 (explicitly excluded from the facility-setting PE calculation, i.e. NOT priced into iud_insertion_professional_fee_facility). Since the bariatric-surgery OR/facility itself is never separately charged to the combined arm under the incremental-cost principle, these supplies are a genuine incremental cost when the IUD insertion is added to that facility setting -- NOT double-counted, unlike if this were (incorrectly) also added to the standalone arm, where it is already bundled into the full office-rate professional fee.

description: Scenario toggle: does the combined strategy require a separate preliminary office visit with the gynecologist (for counseling and consent) before the day of bariatric surgery?
source: Structural modeling convention, not a literature-evidence claim -- matches the pattern used for reference_dollar_year and combined_requires_separate_professional_fee. Mirrors the sibling emb_colonoscopy project's combined_requires_preop_office_visit toggle for its structurally identical D&C arm, confirmed by reading that project's config/model_parameters.csv directly, 2026-09-11: a patient cannot meaningfully consent to a procedure while already under anesthesia for a different one, so the consenting physician (here, the gynecologist, who is not the bariatric surgeon -- see combined_requires_separate_professional_fee) needs their own encounter on an earlier date.
notes: Base case now includes a separate preop office visit (iud_preop_office_visit_cost, added as a component in compute_combined_strategy_cost()). Toggle to FALSE to model consent/risk assessment folded into an existing visit instead (e.g. the patient's own pre-bariatric-surgery multidisciplinary workup, if the gynecologist happens to be part of that team) -- not yet built as a named scenario, but the toggle exists for that purpose.

description: Preoperative history/physical/consent visit cost for combined-arm IUD placement (established patient, CPT 99214)
source: Reused directly from the sibling emb_colonoscopy project's verified extraction (dnc_preop_clinic_visit_cost, confirmed by reading that project's config/model_parameters.csv directly, 2026-09-11): CMS Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service, 2024 (CPT 99214, filtered to Rndrng_Prvdr_Type = 'Obstetrics & Gynecology', live API query 2026-08-28); 7,642 provider-service rows, 515,741 observed services.
notes: Not re-pulled fresh for this project -- reused because the underlying claim (a real-world OB/GYN level-4 E/M visit cost) transfers directly regardless of which procedure prompted the consent discussion. Level 4 (99214, moderate complexity) rather than 99213 (the code office_visit_em_cost uses for the standalone arm's own routine insertion visit) reflects that this is specifically a surgical-consent/risk-discussion encounter, not a routine visit. Checked directly, 2026-09-11: CPT 58300's own CMS global-surgery period is 'XXX' (RVU26C, GLOB DAYS field) -- the global-surgery concept does not apply to this code at all, so there is no bundling rule that would fold a preop visit on an earlier date into the procedure's own fee, unlike CPT 58120's 010-day period in the sibling project (which the sibling project also confirmed does not trigger the 1-day-before bundling rule that applies to 090-day major procedures). Low/high are the real p25/p75 from the same claims data.

description: Median wage for an obstetrician/gynecologist (SOC 29-1218), per minute
source: O*NET OnLine (https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/29-1218.00), median hourly wage $140.82, attributed to BLS 2025 wage data, directly verified 2026-09-11, for SOC 29-1218, Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Same discovery method already used for surgery_scheduler_wage_per_minute (bls.gov itself returns HTTP 403 to automated retrieval; O*NET OnLine republishes the same OEWS wage data without blocking it). Converted to per-minute by dividing by 60: 140.82 / 60 = 2.347.
notes: Used for the combined arm's postop results-discussion cost (combined_arm_postop_discussion_minutes x this wage), not for either arm's actual insertion professional fee, which remains CPT-58300-based (iud_insertion_professional_fee / _facility_ratio). This is a genuinely different cost concept: physician TIME spent on an activity (a phone call) that is not itself a separately billable encounter (no physical exam, not an E/M visit), priced the same way surgery_scheduler_wage_per_minute prices non-clinical staff time, rather than via a CPT/RVU fee.

description: Gynecologist time spent on a postop phone call discussing procedure results with the patient after combined-arm placement
source: User-provided operational estimate (project owner, 2026-09-11): the gynecologist speaks with the patient by phone, separately from the bariatric-surgery recovery course, because the patient cannot meaningfully discuss the IUD placement while under anesthesia and is otherwise occupied recovering from a much larger surgery; no physical examination is needed for the IUD specifically, so this is a phone call rather than an in-person visit. Applies ONLY to the combined arm: the standalone arm's own office visit already includes this discussion live, in the same encounter as the insertion itself (already priced into office_visit_em_cost).
notes: This is a genuinely new cost category this model had not priced at all: the combined arm's device gets placed while the patient is under anesthesia, and IUD insertions do not get a formal, separately-billed postop office visit (confirmed directly, see iud_string_check_followup_not_recommended in this file), so nothing else in the model priced the time this conversation actually takes. Not itself a billable CPT encounter (a phone call with no physical exam is not codeable as a standard E/M visit), so priced as raw physician time via gynecologist_wage_per_minute rather than a procedure fee. No low/high range given (a single operational estimate, not a literature-derived figure) -- excluded from analysis/04_sensitivity_analysis.R's sweep for the same reason as other unranged parameters. Checked directly, not assumed, whether this is already bundled into a global surgical fee: no. CPT 58300's own CMS global-surgery period is 'XXX' (RVU26C, GLOB DAYS field, the same lookup used for iud_preop_office_visit_cost) -- CMS defines 'XXX' as 'global concept does not apply to the code,' so there is no global package for this code at all, pre- or post-op, for the gynecologist billing it. Separately, this call happens on a later calendar day than the insertion (the patient is in the OR, then recovering from the bariatric procedure, that day), so even the general same-day-minor-procedure bundling rule would not apply. The bariatric surgeon's own global period, if any, covers a different physician's different procedure code, not this one.

description: Documents a deliberate decision NOT to model a cost: routine follow-up string-check visits after IUD placement are not recommended practice, for either arm
source: Curtis KM, Nguyen AT, Tepper NK, Zapata LB, Snyder EM, Hatfield-Timajchy K, Kortsmit K, Cohen MA, Whiteman MK. 'U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, 2024.' MMWR Recomm Rep. 2024;73(3):1-77. Published August 8, 2024. Directly verified via https://www.cdc.gov/contraception/hcp/usspr/intrauterine-contraception.html, 2026-09-11: 'No routine follow-up visit is required' after IUD placement. The same page states the evidence behind this is 'very limited and of poor quality' (level of evidence II-2) for any specific follow-up-visit schedule improving continuation, and that clinicians should instead 'consider performing an examination to check for the presence of the IUD strings' opportunistically at other routine visits, not via a dedicated scheduled visit.
notes: Checked directly in response to a user question ('What does the data say about IUD string checks in the office?'). No cost is added to either arm for a routine string-check visit, and this is a deliberate, evidence-based exclusion, not an oversight: current CDC guidance explicitly does not recommend one. Consistent with the user's own observation that IUD inserts typically do not get a postop visit. If a patient-initiated, symptom-driven visit (cannot feel strings, pain, suspected expulsion) is later modeled, that would be a different, separately-justified cost -- not the routine, scheduled visit this CDC guidance addresses.

description: Probability that a patient scheduled for a standalone, separate-visit IUD insertion never returns for it at all (distinct from standalone_office_failure_probability, which covers an ATTEMPTED insertion that fails outright)
source: Baldwin MK, Edelman AB, Lim JY, Nichols MD, Bednarek PH, Jensen JT. 'Comparison of intrauterine device insertion at 3 weeks versus 6 weeks postpartum: a randomized trial.' Contraception. 2016;93(4):356-363. doi:10.1016/j.contraception.2015.12.006. PMID 26686914. Directly verified via the Europe PMC abstract, 2026-09-11. Prospective RCT, 201 postpartum women intending interval IUD placement, randomized to a 3-week (n=101) vs. standard 6-week (n=100) scheduled return visit: 'Most participants returned for IUD placement as scheduled; 70.1% (53/75) in the early group, 74.3% (58/78) in the standard group.' Base/low value is the standard (6-week) group's complement (1 - 0.743 = 0.257); high value is the early (3-week) group's complement (1 - 0.701 = 0.299).
notes: Population mismatch, flagged explicitly: this is a POSTPARTUM population returning for a scheduled interval visit after childbirth, not a bariatric-surgery population; no published loss-to-follow-up data specific to scheduling an IUD visit around bariatric surgery was found. Used as the best available real-world analog for 'does a patient scheduled for a separate, later visit actually show up,' since the underlying logistics phenomenon -- returning for a deliberately scheduled interval procedure after a different major medical event -- is structurally similar. This represents a real, currently UNPRICED effectiveness gap: cost-minimization analysis assumes equal effectiveness across arms by design, so this is NOT folded into either arm's expected_total_cost. See compute_probability_device_placed() in R/strategy_costs.R, and expected_cost_per_referred_patient, for how this is reported separately instead of silently baked into (or omitted from) the headline dollar comparison.
